content: The treatment of infections caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonorrhea) is a critical public health issue due to the increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Gonorrhea is the second most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI) globally, leading to significant morbidity and economic burden. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed updated guidelines to address the challenges posed by evolving resistance patterns and to provide evidence-based recommendations for the treatment of gonococcal infections. Key Points on Gonorrhea and Its Management: 1. Clinical Manifestations: In men, uncomplicated gonococcal infections typically present as urethritis, characterized by urethral discharge and dysuria. In women, the infection may cause mucopurulent cervicitis, though it is often asymptomatic. This asymptomatic nature in women can lead to undiagnosed and untreated infections, resulting in severe complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), ectopic pregnancy, and infertility. Rectal and pharyngeal infections in both men and women are frequently asymptomatic. Untreated urethral infections in men can lead to epididymitis, urethral stricture, and infertility. Neonates born to mothers with gonococcal infections are at risk of developing neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum), which can result in blindness if not treated promptly. 2. Diagnosis: Neisseria gonorrhoeae can be diagnosed using culture methods, nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), or Gram stain (in men with urethritis). In resource-limited settings without laboratory diagnostic support, clinical diagnosis is often based on symptoms such as vaginal or urethral discharge. 3. Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR): The rapid emergence of AMR in N. gonorrhoeae is a significant concern, with high-level resistance to previously recommended quinolones now widespread. Decreased susceptibility to extended-spectrum cephalosporins (e.g., ceftriaxone and cefixime), which are first-line treatments, has been reported in several countries, with documented cases of treatment failure. 4. Treatment Recommendations: The WHO strongly recommends that local antimicrobial resistance data guide the choice of therapy. In settings where local resistance data are unavailable, dual therapy is preferred over single therapy to reduce the risk of treatment failure and further resistance development. Dual Therapy Options: Ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly (IM) as a single dose PLUS azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose. Cefixime 400 mg orally as a single dose PLUS azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose. Single Therapy Options (based on local resistance data confirming susceptibility): Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM as a single dose. Cefixime 400 mg orally as a single dose. Spectinomycin 2 g IM as a single dose. Remarks: Due to emerging resistance data, treatment decisions should rely on reliable local antimicrobial susceptibility data. Alternative single-drug therapies, such as gentamicin or kanamycin, are not recommended due to insufficient surveillance data. 5. Oropharyngeal Gonococcal Infections: Dual therapy is preferred for oropharyngeal infections due to the higher likelihood of treatment failure with single therapy. Recommended dual therapy includes ceftriaxone 250 mg IM as a single dose PLUS azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose. Single therapy with ceftriaxone 250 mg IM as a single dose may be considered if local resistance data confirm susceptibility. 6. Prophylaxis and Neonatal Care: Prophylaxis and treatment of neonatal conjunctivitis caused by N. gonorrhoeae are critical to prevent blindness. Updated topical medications have been suggested for prophylaxis of ophthalmia neonatorum. 7. Rationale for Updated Guidelines: Since the publication of the 2003 WHO guidelines, changes in the epidemiology of STIs and advancements in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment have necessitated updates in gonorrhea management. The updated guidelines aim to address the urgent need for revised treatment recommendations in response to changing AMR patterns. 8. Implementation and Adaptation: Countries are encouraged to incorporate updated global guidance into their national protocols, adapting recommendations to local epidemiological and antimicrobial susceptibility data. 9. Future Directions: Additional modules will address treatments for other STIs, including Chlamydia trachomatis, herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), and Treponema pallidum (syphilis). Future work will also provide guidance on syphilis screening and treatment in pregnant women, syndromic management of STIs, and clinical management of other STIs. 10. Methodology: The guidelines were developed using the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2014) and involved international STI experts, clinicians, researchers, and program managers. Systematic reviews of treatment effectiveness were conducted by a team from McMaster University, and evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Conclusion: The WHO guidelines for the treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae emphasize the importance of evidence-based recommendations tailored to local resistance patterns. Dual therapy is preferred in most cases to mitigate the risk of treatment failure and resistance development. The guidelines also highlight the need for ongoing surveillance, research, and adaptation of national protocols to address the evolving challenges of gonorrhea management.
